summary:
Tripura stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. An estimated two million transgender people live in India.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has interpreted to cover gender identity. The Allahabad High Court extended that prohibition in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 Sakshi Jain, an openly transgender law student, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Within Tripura, transgender travellers have themselves been the object of sustained checkpoint enforcement. Police apprehended 15 Bangladeshi nationals including 7 transgender individuals in separate incidents within 24 hours, searching a bus at the Panisagar checkpoint on the Assam-Agartala highway in North Tripura and finding detainees with fake Aadhaar and PAN cards travelling to Mumbai via Guwahati. On 2 August 2024 at the same Panisagar check post, officers detained 7 Bangladeshi nationals, 2 transgender individuals and 5 others described as disguised as third-gender, bound for Mumbai by bus. On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people: a first group of 6, holding 3 transgender persons, was stopped after midnight en route to Mumbai, and a second group of 6, including 3 children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station, with a local helper, Md Hafizur, arrested for facilitating movement. Tripura shares a 856-km porous border with Bangladesh, and the cases were framed as fraudulent-document and border-crossing offences rather than offences against the detainees' gender.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.
tangentialFactors:
Convictions for immigration and document offences do not indicate hostility to gender identity as such, but the pattern shows that gender presentation in Tripura draws scrutiny at bus and rail checkpoints: detainees were recorded as transgender or as disguised as third-gender in the police accounts themselves, and searches of buses on the Assam-Agartala highway are routine.

Bans on conversion therapy from the Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating elsewhere in India.

Intersex minors remain at risk nationally. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Facilities and welfare machinery are set at state level in India, and Tripura's neighbours illustrate the range: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.
localsOnly:
Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, which reaches residents of Tripura through public hospitals.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Residents arrested in the Tripura checkpoint operations were charged with fraudulent documents and illegal border crossing; the reports do not describe charges relating to gender identity, and one local facilitator was arrested for arranging movement.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tripura-specific transgender welfare board, housing scheme or state surgery programme is sourced in the inventory; the welfare boards described are those of other Indian states, so Tripura's own provision remains unresolved.

The inventory does not state what happened to the transgender detainees after the three checkpoint operations, whether they were deported, detained or released, and whether any complaint of mistreatment followed. That is unresolved.

No source in the inventory reports a trans visitor being refused entry to Tripura on grounds of gender identity, nor any hate-crime or assault figures for Tripura. Absence of such reports in this inventory is not evidence of absence on the ground.

Whether the March 2026 recognition scheme affects how Indian border and police personnel treat a trans person whose documents do not match the socio-cultural categories listed in the amendment is not sourced and remains unresolved.
